ab_petra.blurb: Petra is the busiest and most celebrated wall at Prairie Creek, a limestone sport venue in Kananaskis Country west of Bragg Creek. Ten bolted lines climb steep, pocketed rock that tops out around 18 metres. This is hard-man territory: one route sits in the 5.10s, one in the low 5.11s, six are 5.12, and two reach 5.13, so it suits strong sport climbers rather than beginners. A broad, easily spotted belay terrace below the wall makes it simple to find, and it sits a short uphill scramble beyond the main approach trail. Expect seepage and damp pockets after wet weather.

ab_weeping_wall_area.blurb: The Weeping Wall is a tall band of cliffs, around 300 metres high, at the western foot of Cirrus Mountain, right beside Highway 93 in the north end of Banff National Park, just short of the Jasper boundary. Water streams down the faces through spring and summer, then freezes into big pillars each winter, making this one of the best-known ice venues on the Icefields Parkway. Ten ice lines are listed, from WI3 up to WI6, with the bulk at WI4 and WI5, so there is something for steady leaders and for experts. Roadside setting means short days out and plenty of company in good conditions.

ab_icefields_parkway_north_ice.blurb: This stretch of the Icefields Parkway covers the ice and mixed lines that lie beyond Sunwapta Pass, heading toward Jasper, roughly twenty minutes of driving past the Weeping Wall. Ten ice routes are recorded, running from WI3 to WI6: the largest share are WI3 and WI4, with a handful of WI5 and a single WI6 for those wanting a serious outing. Several are multi-pitch waterfalls of about three rope lengths, and a few combine ice with mixed ground. The setting is high and open at the edge of the icefield country, so check winter weather before driving the parkway.

ab_north_face.blurb: North Face is a sector of Little Russia, a steep limestone sport area in Peskett canyon along the David Thompson Highway near Nordegg. Ten bolted lines are packed into a stream-cut wall, with grades from 5.11 through 5.13 and most of them at 5.12. The climbing is mostly vertical and finishes on gentle slab. It lies on the shadier, harder side of the canyon and stays cold; the rushing creek makes it hard to keep ropes dry and drowns out voices at the anchors, so agree on a lowering plan beforehand. Seepage is common early in the season and after heavy rain.
